chapters.chapterName: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe

tests.title: Rise of Nationalism in Europe – Test 1 (Basics)

questions.questionText: Who prepared a series of four prints in 1848 visualising his dream of a world made up of democratic and social Republics?
questions.hint: He was a French artist working in the year of revolutions.
questions.explanation: Frédéric Sorrieu, a French artist, prepared four prints in 1848 showing peoples of the world grouped as distinct nations, offering homage to the statue of Liberty.

questions.questionText: The first clear expression of nationalism in Europe came with the French Revolution of:
questions.hint: It is the revolution that overthrew the French monarchy.
questions.explanation: The French Revolution of 1789 transferred sovereignty from the monarchy to the body of French citizens and produced the first clear expression of nationalism.

questions.questionText: Which of the following was NOT a measure taken by the French revolutionaries to create a sense of collective identity?
questions.optionA: The Estates General was renamed the National Assembly
questions.optionB: A centralised administrative system with uniform laws for all citizens
questions.optionC: The restoration of the Bourbon monarchy
questions.optionD: A new hymn and a new French flag, the tricolour
questions.hint: One of these undid the Revolution rather than advancing it.
questions.explanation: The Bourbon monarchy was restored much later, by the Congress of Vienna in 1815. The other three were revolutionary measures that built a sense of collective belonging.

questions.questionText: The Civil Code of 1804, usually known as the Napoleonic Code, did away with:
questions.optionB: the use of a common currency
questions.hint: Think about what the Code replaced the old social order with.
questions.explanation: The Napoleonic Code abolished all privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property.

questions.questionText: The Congress of Vienna in 1815 was hosted by:
questions.hint: He was the Austrian Chancellor of the time.
questions.explanation: The Congress of Vienna was hosted by the Austrian Chancellor Duke Metternich, where the European powers drew up a settlement after the defeat of Napoleon.

questions.questionText: Giuseppe Mazzini founded the underground society Young Italy in:
questions.hint: It was founded in a French port city, not in Italy itself.
questions.explanation: Mazzini, an Italian revolutionary born in Genoa, founded Young Italy in Marseilles and Young Europe in Berne.

questions.questionText: The term 'plebiscite' means:
questions.optionA: a written constitution granted by a monarch
questions.optionC: a direct vote by which all the people of a region accept or reject a proposal
questions.hint: The word describes a way of consulting an entire population directly.
questions.explanation: A plebiscite is a direct vote by which all the people of a region are asked to accept or reject a proposal.

questions.questionText: Which allegorical figure was used to represent the French Republic?
questions.hint: The name was a popular Christian first name in France.
questions.explanation: Marianne, a female allegory, personified the French Republic. Her characteristics were drawn from those of Liberty and the Republic, and her statues were erected in public squares.

questions.questionText: Germania, the allegory of the German nation, is shown wearing a crown of:
questions.hint: The plant chosen stands for heroism.
questions.explanation: Germania wears a crown of oak leaves, because the German oak stands for heroism.

questions.questionText: The Act of Union of 1707 between England and Scotland resulted in the formation of:
questions.optionB: the United Kingdom of Great Britain
questions.hint: Recall which two nations the Act joined together.
questions.explanation: The Act of Union of 1707 between England and Scotland created the United Kingdom of Great Britain, in which England was able to impose its influence on Scotland.

tests.title: Rise of Nationalism in Europe – Test 2 (Liberalism & Romanticism)

questions.questionText: In the early nineteenth century in Europe, the term 'liberalism' stood for:
questions.optionA: freedom for the individual and equality of all before the law
questions.optionB: the preservation of monarchy and the Church
questions.optionD: the rule of the landed aristocracy
questions.hint: The word comes from the Latin root liber, meaning free.
questions.explanation: Liberalism derived from the Latin root liber, meaning free. Politically it stressed government by consent, an end to autocracy and clerical privileges, a constitution and representative government.

questions.questionText: In the territories he conquered, Napoleon's administration introduced:
questions.optionB: the abolition of the feudal system and freedom from serfdom
questions.optionC: the restoration of the privileges of the nobility
questions.hint: Consider what happened to peasants under his rule.
questions.explanation: In the areas Napoleon conquered, the administration abolished the feudal system and freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues, besides removing guild restrictions in the towns.

questions.questionText: Which social group was the dominant class on the European continent in the mid-eighteenth century?
questions.hint: Their power rested on ownership of estates in the countryside.
questions.explanation: Socially and politically, a landed aristocracy was the dominant class on the continent, owning estates in the countryside and town houses, though it was numerically a small group.

questions.questionText: The Zollverein, formed in 1834 at the initiative of Prussia, was a:
questions.optionD: customs union that abolished tariff barriers
questions.hint: The name refers to duties charged on goods.
questions.explanation: The Zollverein was a customs union formed in 1834 at Prussia's initiative. It abolished tariff barriers among the German states and reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two.

questions.questionText: Greece gained recognition as an independent nation through the Treaty of:
questions.hint: The treaty was named after the Ottoman capital.
questions.explanation: The Treaty of Constantinople of 1832 recognised Greece as an independent nation, after a struggle for independence that began in 1821.

questions.questionText: Which English poet died of fever while fighting in the Greek war of independence?
questions.hint: He organised funds and went to fight himself.
questions.explanation: The English poet Lord Byron organised funds and later went to fight in the Greek war of independence, where he died of fever in 1824.

questions.questionText: Johann Gottfried Herder claimed that true German culture was to be discovered among:
questions.hint: He looked to folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances.
questions.explanation: Herder, a German philosopher, claimed that true German culture was to be discovered among the common people — das volk — through their folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances.

questions.questionText: The term 'volksgeist' means:
questions.optionA: the union of church and state
questions.optionD: the true spirit of the nation
questions.hint: It refers to a nation's inner character, expressed through its culture.
questions.explanation: Volksgeist means the true spirit of the nation. Romantic nationalists argued that it was carried in the folk culture of a people.

questions.questionText: The Grimm Brothers of Germany are best known for collecting:
questions.hint: Their collection was published in six volumes from 1812.
questions.explanation: Grimm's Fairy Tales, a collection of folk tales published in six volumes from 1812, was part of the effort to recover and preserve the national spirit through popular culture.

questions.questionText: In 1845, the weavers of Silesia revolted against:
questions.optionB: contractors who drastically reduced their payments
questions.hint: Their anger was directed at the men who supplied raw material and took the finished cloth.
questions.explanation: The Silesian weavers led a revolt in 1845 against contractors who supplied them raw material and gave orders for finished textiles but drastically reduced their payments.

tests.title: Rise of Nationalism in Europe – Test 3 (Unification & Revolutions)

questions.questionText: The February revolution of 1848 in France led to:
questions.optionA: the abdication of the monarch and the proclamation of a Republic
questions.optionB: the creation of the German Confederation
questions.optionC: the signing of the Treaty of Vienna
questions.optionD: the return of Louis Philippe to the throne
questions.hint: The event ended the reign of the Orleanist monarch.
questions.explanation: In February 1848 food shortages and unemployment brought the people of Paris onto the streets. Louis Philippe was forced to flee, a Republic was proclaimed and suffrage was granted to all adult males above 21.

questions.questionText: The Frankfurt Parliament of 1848 assembled in the:
questions.hint: The deputies met in a church building.
questions.explanation: On 18 May 1848, 831 elected representatives took their places in the Church of St Paul in Frankfurt and drafted a constitution for a German nation headed by a monarchy subject to a parliament.

questions.questionText: The crown offered by the Frankfurt Parliament was refused by:
questions.optionC: Friedrich Wilhelm IV, King of Prussia
questions.hint: The Prussian king rejected it and sided with the other monarchs.
questions.explanation: Friedrich Wilhelm IV, King of Prussia, rejected the crown offered by the Frankfurt Parliament and joined other monarchs in opposing the elected assembly.

questions.questionText: Who described Mazzini as 'the most dangerous enemy of our social order'?
questions.hint: The remark came from the architect of the conservative order after 1815.
questions.explanation: Metternich, alarmed by Mazzini's opposition to monarchy and his vision of democratic republics, described him as the most dangerous enemy of the social order.

questions.questionText: Who was the Chief Minister of Sardinia-Piedmont who engineered a diplomatic alliance with France?
questions.hint: He was neither a revolutionary nor a democrat, but a skilled diplomat.
questions.explanation: Count Cavour, Chief Minister of Sardinia-Piedmont, engineered a careful diplomatic alliance with France that enabled Sardinia-Piedmont to defeat the Austrian forces in 1859.

questions.questionText: Giuseppe Garibaldi's band of armed volunteers was known as the:
questions.hint: They were named after the colour of the shirts they wore.
questions.explanation: Garibaldi led armed volunteers known as the Red Shirts, who marched into South Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in 1860 and drove out the Spanish rulers.

questions.questionText: In 1861, who was proclaimed king of a united Italy?
questions.hint: He was the ruler of Sardinia-Piedmont.
questions.explanation: In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II, the ruler of Sardinia-Piedmont, was proclaimed king of united Italy.

questions.questionText: In January 1871, the Prussian king William I was proclaimed German Emperor at:
questions.hint: The ceremony was held in a French palace after the war with France.
questions.explanation: On 18 January 1871 an assembly of German princes, army representatives and ministers gathered in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles and proclaimed the Prussian king William I as German Emperor.

questions.questionText: Bismarck's method of achieving German unification is best described as:
questions.optionA: a war carried out by Prussian army and bureaucracy
questions.optionB: a series of plebiscites in the German states
questions.optionC: a peaceful union agreed at the Frankfurt Parliament
questions.optionD: a popular revolution led by the middle classes
questions.hint: The process was led from above, not from below.
questions.explanation: The unification of Germany was carried out by Otto von Bismarck with the help of the Prussian army and bureaucracy, through three wars over seven years with Austria, Denmark and France.

questions.questionText: Which region was described as the 'powder keg of Europe' in the early twentieth century?
questions.hint: The area was made up of many small states under Ottoman rule.
questions.explanation: The Balkans, a region of great ethnic variation under Ottoman rule, became an area of intense conflict as its peoples claimed independence and the great powers competed there. It came to be called the powder keg of Europe.

tests.title: Rise of Nationalism in Europe – Test 4 (Mixed & Application)

questions.questionText: The idea of 'la patrie' and 'le citoyen' in revolutionary France emphasised:
questions.optionB: the fatherland and a united community of citizens with equal rights
questions.optionC: the authority of the Catholic Church
questions.hint: The two terms translate as the fatherland and the citizen.
questions.explanation: The ideas of la patrie (the fatherland) and le citoyen (the citizen) emphasised the notion of a united community enjoying equal rights under a constitution.

questions.questionText: Which of the following was an outcome of the Congress of Vienna, 1815?
questions.optionC: The Bourbon dynasty was restored to power in France
questions.hint: The settlement tried to undo the changes of the previous twenty-five years.
questions.explanation: The Vienna settlement of 1815 restored the Bourbon dynasty in France, set up a series of states on France's boundaries to prevent future expansion, and sought to restore the conservative order.

questions.questionText: Ernst Renan, in his 1882 lecture 'What is a Nation?', argued that the existence of a nation is:
questions.optionA: a daily plebiscite, resting on the consent of its people
questions.optionB: determined by the strength of its army
questions.optionD: a matter of race and religion alone
questions.hint: He believed a nation must be continually willed by those who belong to it.
questions.explanation: Renan argued that a nation is the culmination of a long past of endeavours, sacrifice and devotion, and that its existence is a daily plebiscite — it depends on the continuing consent of its people.

questions.questionText: After 1815, the ideology of conservatism stood for:
questions.optionA: the abolition of monarchy and the Church
questions.optionB: the preservation of traditional institutions such as monarchy, Church and the family
questions.optionC: universal adult suffrage in every state
questions.optionD: the immediate unification of Germany and Italy
questions.hint: Think about what the powers meeting at Vienna wanted to hold on to.
questions.explanation: Conservatives after 1815 believed that established traditional institutions — monarchy, the Church, social hierarchies, property and the family — should be preserved, though most accepted that some modernisation could strengthen them.

questions.questionText: Bismarck fought three wars over seven years to unify Germany. Which of the following was NOT one of those wars?
questions.hint: Recall the three states Prussia defeated between 1864 and 1871.
questions.explanation: The three wars were fought with Austria, Denmark and France. Prussia did not fight Russia during the process of German unification.

questions.questionText: Which of the following pairs of allegory and nation is correctly matched?
questions.hint: Match each female figure to the country whose republic or nation she personified.
questions.explanation: Britannia is the allegory of Britain, Marianne of France and Germania of the German nation, so only Britannia and Britain are correctly paired.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the Habsburg Empire that ruled over Austria-Hungary is correct?
questions.optionA: It was a patchwork of many different regions and peoples with no common identity
questions.optionB: It was a democratic republic governed by an elected parliament
questions.optionC: It consisted only of German-speaking territories
questions.optionD: It was a homogeneous nation with a single language
questions.hint: Consider the variety of peoples the Habsburgs ruled over.
questions.explanation: The Habsburg Empire was a patchwork of many different regions and peoples, including Alpine and Italian-speaking provinces, Bohemia, Galicia and Hungary. The only tie holding them together was a common ruler.

questions.questionText: The 1848 revolutions saw women form political associations, but the Frankfurt Parliament:
questions.optionB: allowed women only to stand in the visitors' gallery as observers
questions.optionC: banned women from the city of Frankfurt
questions.optionD: gave women the right to vote
questions.hint: Women took part in the events but were denied political rights.
questions.explanation: Although women had formed political associations, founded newspapers and taken part in the 1848 demonstrations, they were denied suffrage during the election of the Assembly and were admitted to the Frankfurt Parliament only as observers in the visitors' gallery.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): After 1871, nationalism in Europe became narrow and intolerant.
Reason (R): The major European powers increasingly used nationalism to promote their own imperialist aims.
questions.optionA: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionB: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionC: A is true, but R is false.
questions.optionD: A is false, but R is true.
questions.hint: Consider how the great powers used national feeling in the decades before 1914.
questions.explanation: Nationalism after 1871 no longer retained its earlier idealistic and liberal character. The major powers manipulated national feeling to further their imperialist ambitions, which contributed to the outbreak of the First World War. Both statements are true and R explains A.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): Napoleon's rule was welcomed everywhere in the territories he conquered.
Reason (R): The Napoleonic Code abolished privileges based on birth and established equality before the law.
questions.optionA: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionB: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionC: A is true, but R is false.
questions.optionD: A is false, but R is true.
questions.hint: Weigh the benefits of Napoleon's reforms against the loss of political freedom.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: initial enthusiasm soon turned to hostility, as increased taxation, censorship, forced conscription and loss of political freedom outweighed the advantages of the new administration. The reason is a correct statement about the Code.

tests.title: Nationalism in India – Test 1 (Basics)

questions.questionText: The Rowlatt Act, which gave the government enormous powers to repress political activities, was passed in:
questions.hint: It was passed in the same year as the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
questions.explanation: The Rowlatt Act was hurriedly passed through the Imperial Legislative Council in 1919, allowing detention of political prisoners without trial for two years.

questions.questionText: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on:
questions.hint: It happened on Baisakhi day in Amritsar.
questions.explanation: On 13 April 1919 a large crowd gathered in the enclosed ground of Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, where General Dyer blocked the exit and ordered his troops to fire, killing hundreds.

questions.questionText: Who ordered the firing on the crowd at Jallianwala Bagh?
questions.hint: He later said his object was to produce a moral effect.
questions.explanation: General Dyer entered the Jallianwala Bagh, blocked the exit points and ordered his troops to fire on the crowd, killing hundreds of people.

questions.questionText: The Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in:
questions.hint: It was formed in the same year as the Rowlatt Act.
questions.explanation: A Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919 to defend the temporal powers of the Ottoman Sultan, the Khalifa, after the defeat of Ottoman Turkey.

questions.questionText: Which two brothers were among the leaders of the Khilafat movement?
questions.optionC: Lala Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal
questions.optionD: Ashfaqullah Khan and Ram Prasad Bismil
questions.hint: They worked closely with Mahatma Gandhi in 1920.
questions.explanation: The brothers Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali were among the young Muslim leaders who, along with Mahatma Gandhi, built a united mass action on the Khilafat question.

questions.questionText: Mahatma Gandhi's idea of satyagraha emphasised:
questions.optionB: the power of truth and the need to search for truth
questions.optionD: the boycott of all Indian-made goods
questions.hint: The word itself combines truth with insistence.
questions.explanation: Satyagraha emphasised the power of truth and the need to search for truth. It suggested that a satyagrahi could win a battle through non-violence, by appealing to the conscience of the oppressor.

questions.questionText: Mahatma Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, organised in 1917, was in:
questions.hint: It was in Bihar, among peasants of an indigo-growing district.
questions.explanation: In 1917 Gandhi travelled to Champaran in Bihar to inspire the peasants to struggle against the oppressive plantation system.

questions.questionText: In 1917 Gandhi organised a satyagraha in Kheda district of Gujarat in support of:
questions.optionD: peasants affected by crop failure and plague who demanded relaxation in revenue collection
questions.hint: The district had been struck by both crop failure and an epidemic.
questions.explanation: The peasants of Kheda, affected by crop failure and a plague epidemic, could not pay the revenue and demanded that revenue collection be relaxed. Gandhi organised a satyagraha to support them.

questions.questionText: The Non-Cooperation programme was adopted at the Congress session held in December 1920 at:
questions.hint: It followed the earlier session at Calcutta in September 1920.
questions.explanation: At the Congress session at Nagpur in December 1920, the Non-Cooperation programme was adopted after being introduced at the Calcutta session in September 1920.

questions.questionText: The word 'swaraj' means:
questions.hint: It combines the words for self and rule.
questions.explanation: Swaraj means self-rule. It became the central demand of the national movement and was later defined as Purna Swaraj, or complete independence.

tests.title: Nationalism in India – Test 2 (Movements & Milestones)

questions.questionText: In 'Hind Swaraj' (1909), Mahatma Gandhi declared that British rule had survived in India because:
questions.optionB: the British army was too strong to resist
questions.hint: His argument placed responsibility on Indians themselves.
questions.explanation: In Hind Swaraj Gandhi declared that British rule was established in India with the cooperation of Indians, and had survived only because of this cooperation. If Indians refused to cooperate, British rule in India would collapse within a year.

questions.questionText: Mahatma Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922 after the violent incident at:
questions.hint: A procession there turned violent and a police station was set on fire.
questions.explanation: Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922 after a procession at Chauri Chaura turned violent, feeling that satyagrahis needed proper training before they were ready for mass struggles.

questions.questionText: The Simon Commission, which arrived in India in 1928, was opposed because:
questions.optionC: it did not have a single Indian member
questions.optionD: it proposed to abolish the Congress
questions.hint: The objection was about who sat on the Commission.
questions.explanation: The Statutory Commission under Sir John Simon had not a single Indian member, so all parties including the Congress and the Muslim League participated in demonstrations greeting it with the slogan 'Go back Simon'.

questions.questionText: At the Lahore Congress session of December 1929, the demand for 'Purna Swaraj' was formalised under the presidency of:
questions.hint: The president was the younger of the two Nehrus.
questions.explanation: Under the presidency of Jawaharlal Nehru, the Lahore Congress session of December 1929 formalised the demand of Purna Swaraj, or full independence for India.

questions.questionText: Which date was declared as Independence Day by the Congress in 1930?
questions.hint: The date was later adopted for another national purpose.
questions.explanation: 26 January 1930 was declared Independence Day, when people were to take a pledge to struggle for complete independence.

questions.questionText: Mahatma Gandhi began the Salt March on 12 March 1930 from:
questions.hint: He set out from his own ashram near Ahmedabad.
questions.explanation: Gandhi started his famous Salt March accompanied by 78 volunteers from his ashram at Sabarmati to the coastal town of Dandi.

questions.questionText: The Salt March covered a distance of approximately:
questions.hint: The marchers walked for about 24 days at roughly 10 miles a day.
questions.explanation: The march covered over 240 miles from Sabarmati to Dandi. The volunteers walked for 24 days, about 10 miles a day.

questions.questionText: Mahatma Gandhi ceremonially violated the salt law on:
questions.hint: It happened on reaching the coast, weeks after the march began.
questions.explanation: On 6 April 1930 Gandhi reached Dandi and ceremonially violated the law, manufacturing salt by boiling sea water.

questions.questionText: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on:
questions.hint: It was signed shortly before Gandhi went to London.
questions.explanation: On 5 March 1931 Gandhi signed a pact with Viceroy Irwin, agreeing to participate in a Round Table Conference in London in return for the release of political prisoners.

questions.questionText: The Second Round Table Conference, attended by Mahatma Gandhi, was held in London in:
questions.hint: It took place in the winter following the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
questions.explanation: Gandhi travelled to London for the Second Round Table Conference in December 1931, but the negotiations broke down and he returned disappointed.

tests.title: Nationalism in India – Test 3 (Peasants, Workers & Culture)

questions.questionText: The militant guerrilla movement in the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh was led by:
questions.hint: His followers believed he had special powers and could survive bullet shots.
questions.explanation: Alluri Sitaram Raju led the militant guerrilla movement in the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh in the early 1920s. He was captured and executed in 1924.

questions.questionText: The peasant movement in Awadh was led by:
questions.hint: He was a sanyasi who had earlier been an indentured labourer in Fiji.
questions.explanation: Baba Ramchandra, a sanyasi who had earlier been to Fiji as an indentured labourer, led the peasant movement in Awadh against talukdars and landlords.

questions.questionText: The Oudh Kisan Sabha was set up in October 1920 by:
questions.optionC: Jawaharlal Nehru, Baba Ramchandra and a few others
questions.optionD: Alluri Sitaram Raju and his followers
questions.hint: One of the founders later became India's first Prime Minister.
questions.explanation: The Oudh Kisan Sabha was set up in October 1920, headed by Jawaharlal Nehru, Baba Ramchandra and a few others. Within a month over 300 branches had been set up in the villages around the region.

questions.questionText: Under the Inland Emigration Act of 1859, plantation workers in Assam:
questions.optionA: were given land of their own
questions.optionB: could return home once every year
questions.optionC: were paid wages fixed by the government
questions.optionD: were not permitted to leave the tea gardens without permission
questions.hint: The Act restricted their freedom of movement.
questions.explanation: Under the Inland Emigration Act of 1859, plantation workers were not permitted to leave the tea gardens without permission, and such permission was rarely granted.

questions.questionText: The famous image of Bharat Mata was first painted in 1905 by:
questions.hint: The painter was the nephew of Rabindranath Tagore.
questions.explanation: Abanindranath Tagore painted his famous image of Bharat Mata in 1905, portraying her as an ascetic figure, calm, composed, divine and spiritual.

questions.questionText: 'Vande Mataram', later included in the novel Anandamath, was written by:
questions.hint: The hymn to the motherland was composed in the 1870s.
questions.explanation: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote 'Vande Mataram' as a hymn to the motherland in the 1870s. It was later included in his novel Anandamath and was widely sung during the Swadeshi movement.

questions.questionText: The swaraj flag designed by Mahatma Gandhi in 1921 carried:
questions.optionA: a green field with a white crescent
questions.optionB: eight lotuses and a crescent moon
questions.optionC: three colours and a spinning wheel at the centre
questions.hint: The central emblem stood for self-help.
questions.explanation: By 1921 Gandhi had designed the swaraj flag: a tricolour of red, green and white with a spinning wheel in the centre, representing the Gandhian ideal of self-help.

questions.questionText: Who compiled a four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales called 'The Folklore of Southern India'?
questions.hint: He believed folklore was the people's own literature.
questions.explanation: Natesa Sastri published a massive four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales, The Folklore of Southern India, believing that folklore was national literature and the most trustworthy expression of people's real thoughts.

questions.questionText: The Poona Pact of September 1932 gave the Depressed Classes:
questions.optionA: reserved seats in provincial and central legislative councils, voted in by the general electorate
questions.optionC: a separate province of their own
questions.hint: The settlement replaced one form of representation with another.
questions.explanation: The Poona Pact of September 1932 gave the Depressed Classes reserved seats in provincial and central legislative councils, but they were to be voted in by the general electorate rather than through separate electorates.

questions.questionText: The Depressed Classes Association was founded in 1930 by:
questions.hint: He later clashed with Gandhi at the Second Round Table Conference.
questions.explanation: Dr B.R. Ambedkar organised the Depressed Classes into the Depressed Classes Association in 1930 and clashed with Mahatma Gandhi at the Second Round Table Conference by demanding separate electorates for dalits.

tests.title: Nationalism in India – Test 4 (Mixed & Application)

questions.questionText: Rich peasant communities such as the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh joined the Civil Disobedience Movement mainly because:
questions.optionA: they wanted a share in the colonial administration
questions.optionC: they were hard hit by the trade depression and demanded a reduction in revenue
questions.optionD: they opposed the use of khadi
questions.hint: Their grievance concerned falling agricultural prices.
questions.explanation: Rich peasant communities were hard hit by the trade depression and falling prices. Their cash income disappeared and they refused to pay the government's revenue demand, becoming enthusiastic supporters of the movement.

questions.questionText: The Federation of the Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industries (FICCI) was formed in:
questions.hint: It was formed a few years after the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress.
questions.explanation: Indian industrialists formed the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress in 1920 and the Federation of the Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industries (FICCI) in 1927 to organise their business interests.

questions.questionText: Which of the following was among the eleven demands Mahatma Gandhi placed before Viceroy Irwin on 31 January 1930?
questions.hint: One demand touched every household, rich and poor alike.
questions.explanation: Among the eleven demands was the abolition of the salt tax. Salt was consumed by rich and poor alike and was one of the most essential items of food, which made it a powerful symbol for uniting the nation.

questions.questionText: The practice of 'begar', against which peasants in Awadh protested, meant:
questions.optionB: labour at the landlords' farms without any payment
questions.hint: The word describes work done for nothing.
questions.explanation: Peasants in Awadh had to do begar, that is, work at the landlords' farms without any payment, in addition to paying exorbitant rents and other cesses.

questions.questionText: How did the Civil Disobedience Movement differ from the Non-Cooperation Movement?
questions.optionA: It was led by the Muslim League
questions.optionB: It was confined only to the cities
questions.optionC: People were now asked to break colonial laws, not merely refuse cooperation
questions.optionD: It did not involve the boycott of foreign cloth
questions.hint: Compare refusing to take part with actively defying the law.
questions.explanation: In the Civil Disobedience Movement people were asked not just to refuse cooperation with the British, as in 1921-22, but also to break colonial laws.

questions.questionText: Why did the image of Bharat Mata help develop a sense of nationalism?
questions.optionB: It was printed on colonial currency
questions.optionC: It was approved by the colonial government
questions.optionD: Devotion to this mother figure came to be seen as evidence of one's nationalism
questions.hint: Consider what such a shared image asked of those who saw it.
questions.explanation: Images of Bharat Mata created a figure through which people could imagine the nation. Devotion to this mother figure came to be seen as evidence of one's nationalism.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements about the Non-Cooperation Movement in the towns is correct?
questions.optionA: Foreign goods were boycotted and imports of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922
questions.optionB: Students and teachers refused to join the movement
questions.optionC: Lawyers continued their practice without interruption
questions.optionD: Council elections were boycotted in every province without exception
questions.hint: One measurable effect of the boycott can be seen in trade figures.
questions.explanation: The movement began with middle-class participation in the cities. Foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops picketed and foreign cloth burnt. The import of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922, its value dropping from Rs 102 crore to Rs 57 crore.

questions.questionText: The Swaraj Party, which argued for a return to council politics, was formed by:
questions.optionC: Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose
questions.hint: Both leaders were prominent Congressmen and lawyers.
questions.explanation: Within the Congress, C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party and argued for a return to council politics after the Non-Cooperation Movement was withdrawn.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): Mahatma Gandhi called off the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922.
Reason (R): He felt the movement was turning violent and that satyagrahis needed to be properly trained before they were ready for mass struggles.
questions.optionA: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionB: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionC: A is true, but R is false.
questions.optionD: A is false, but R is true.
questions.hint: Recall what happened at Chauri Chaura and how Gandhi responded to it.
questions.explanation: After the violence at Chauri Chaura, Gandhi withdrew the movement, believing that it was turning violent and that satyagrahis needed proper training before mass struggles. Both statements are true and R explains A.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): The Poona Pact of September 1932 gave the Depressed Classes reserved seats in provincial and central legislative councils.
Reason (R): Dr B.R. Ambedkar organised the dalits into the Depressed Classes Association in 1930.
questions.optionA: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionB: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionC: A is true, but R is false.
questions.optionD: A is false, but R is true.
questions.hint: Both statements are correct, but check whether the second one explains the first.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true. However, the Poona Pact resulted from Gandhi's fast unto death against separate electorates, not from the founding of the Depressed Classes Association two years earlier. R does not explain A.

chapters.chapterName: The Making of a Global World

tests.title: Making of a Global World – Test 1 (Board Scope – Pre-modern World)

questions.questionText: The silk routes are so named because:
questions.optionA: Chinese silk cargoes travelled westward along these routes
questions.optionB: the roads were paved with silk
questions.optionD: silk was the only item ever traded on them
questions.hint: The name comes from the most famous cargo carried west.
questions.explanation: Historians have identified several silk routes over land and sea, knitting together vast regions of Asia and linking Asia with Europe and northern Africa. They are so named after the westward flow of Chinese silk cargoes.

questions.questionText: The silk routes are known to have existed:
questions.optionB: before the Christian era and thriving almost till the fifteenth century
questions.hint: They are among the oldest trade networks in the world.
questions.explanation: The silk routes are known to have existed since before the Christian era and thrived almost till the fifteenth century.

questions.questionText: Besides trade goods, what else travelled along the silk routes?
questions.hint: Consider what missionaries and preachers carried with them.
questions.explanation: Early Christian missionaries and later Muslim preachers travelled this route to Asia, and Buddhism emerged from eastern India and spread in several directions through intersecting points on the silk routes.

questions.questionText: Which goods travelled westwards from India along the silk routes?
questions.hint: India was known for what it grew and what it wove.
questions.explanation: Chinese pottery travelled the same route, as did textiles and spices from India and Southeast Asia.

questions.questionText: In return for goods from Asia, what flowed from Europe along the silk routes?
questions.optionA: Precious metals such as gold and silver
questions.hint: Europe paid for Asian goods in a particular form.
questions.explanation: In return, precious metals — gold and silver — flowed from Europe to Asia in exchange for Asian goods.

questions.questionText: Which of the following reached the rest of the world only after Europeans reached the Americas?
questions.hint: Three of these were long grown in the Old World.
questions.explanation: Many common foods such as potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes were not known to our ancestors until about five centuries ago. They came to Europe and Asia only after Columbus accidentally reached the Americas.

questions.questionText: According to one common belief, noodles travelled west from China and became:
questions.hint: The result is one of Italy's best-known dishes.
questions.explanation: It is believed that noodles travelled west from China to become spaghetti. Another possibility is that Arab traders took pasta to fifth-century Sicily.

questions.questionText: The introduction of the potato greatly improved the diet of Europe's poor. Which country suffered a devastating famine when its potato crop failed?
questions.hint: The country's poor had become heavily dependent on a single crop.
questions.explanation: Ireland's poorest peasants had become so dependent on potatoes that when disease destroyed the crop in the mid-1840s, hundreds of thousands died of starvation.

questions.questionText: Which is the best conclusion to draw from the Irish potato famine of the 1840s?
questions.optionA: New crops always improve the diet of the poor
questions.optionB: Heavy dependence on a single crop can leave a population dangerously vulnerable
questions.optionC: Potatoes were unsuitable for European soil
questions.hint: Consider what happened when the one crop the poor relied on failed.
questions.explanation: Ireland's poorest peasants had become so dependent on potatoes that when disease destroyed the crop in the mid-1840s, hundreds of thousands died of starvation. It shows the danger of relying on a single crop.

questions.questionText: The pre-modern world shrank greatly in the sixteenth century because:
questions.optionB: European sailors found a sea route to Asia and also crossed the ocean to America
questions.hint: Think about the voyages that opened new ocean routes.
questions.explanation: The world changed profoundly in the sixteenth century after European sailors found a sea route to Asia and successfully crossed the western ocean to America.

tests.title: Making of a Global World – Test 2 (Board Scope – Conquest, Disease and Trade)

questions.questionText: Columbus's voyage of 1492 led Europeans to:
questions.hint: He was seeking one destination but reached another.
questions.explanation: In 1492 Columbus set sail westward and reached what we know today as the Americas, a vast continent previously unknown to Europeans.

questions.questionText: The most powerful weapon of the Spanish conquerors of America was not a conventional military weapon at all. It was:
questions.hint: The conquerors carried it on their persons without knowing it.
questions.explanation: The most powerful weapon of the Spanish conquerors was not a conventional military weapon at all. It was the germs of smallpox that they carried on their person.

questions.questionText: Why were America's original inhabitants so vulnerable to smallpox?
questions.optionA: The disease was far more severe in warm climates
questions.optionB: They had no medicines of any kind
questions.optionC: They had been isolated from the rest of the world for millions of years and had no immunity
questions.hint: Immunity depends on prior exposure over generations.
questions.explanation: America's original inhabitants had no immunity against diseases that came from Europe, because they had been cut off from the rest of the world for millions of years. Smallpox proved a deadly killer.

questions.questionText: Precious metals, particularly silver, from mines in present-day Peru and Mexico:
questions.optionA: were shipped to China as tribute
questions.optionB: had little effect on world trade
questions.optionC: were used only for local ornaments
questions.optionD: enhanced Europe's wealth and financed its trade with Asia
questions.hint: Consider how Europe paid for goods from Asia.
questions.explanation: Precious metals, particularly silver, from mines located in present-day Peru and Mexico enhanced Europe's wealth and financed its trade with Asia.

questions.questionText: The legend of El Dorado referred to:
questions.optionA: the fabled city of gold in South America
questions.optionC: a spice island in Southeast Asia
questions.hint: It drew expedition after expedition into South America.
questions.explanation: Legends spread in seventeenth-century Europe about South America's fabled wealth. El Dorado, the fabled city of gold, drew many expeditions in search of it.

questions.questionText: Until the eighteenth century, which two countries were among the richest in the world and pre-eminent in Asian trade?
questions.hint: Both are in Asia and both later declined in relative terms.
questions.explanation: Until the eighteenth century China and India were among the world's richest countries. They were also pre-eminent in Asian trade.

questions.questionText: From the fifteenth century, the conquest of America was led by:
questions.hint: Both were Iberian sea powers.
questions.explanation: The Portuguese and Spanish conquest and colonisation of America was decisively under way by the mid-sixteenth century.

questions.questionText: China's reduced role in world trade from the fifteenth century onwards was mainly because:
questions.optionD: it restricted overseas contacts and retreated into isolation
questions.hint: The change came from a policy decision, not a defeat.
questions.explanation: From the fifteenth century China is said to have restricted overseas contacts and retreated into isolation. Its reduced role, along with the rising importance of the Americas, gradually moved the centre of world trade westwards.

questions.questionText: One consequence of the westward shift in the centre of world trade was that:
questions.optionA: Europe emerged as the centre of world trade
questions.optionC: world trade came to a halt
questions.optionD: Asia became the centre of world trade
questions.hint: Consider which region gained as China's role shrank.
questions.explanation: China's reduced role and the rising importance of the Americas gradually moved the centre of world trade westwards. Europe now emerged as the centre of world trade.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the pre-modern world is correct?
questions.optionA: It involved the exchange of goods alone
questions.optionB: Trade, migration, the movement of capital and even disease-carrying germs were all part of it
questions.optionC: Long-distance contact was limited to Europe
questions.optionD: Global exchange began only in the nineteenth century
questions.hint: Think about everything that moved along the trade routes, not just cargo.
questions.explanation: Before the modern age, trade routes carried far more than goods. Traders and travellers introduced new crops, and the flows also included the movement of people, capital and germs, as the spread of disease to America showed.

tests.title: Making of a Global World – Test 3 (Beyond Board Scope – Project Work)

questions.questionText: The Corn Laws in Britain restricted:
questions.hint: The laws protected British landed interests from cheaper foreign grain.
questions.explanation: The laws allowing the British government to restrict the import of corn are commonly known as the Corn Laws. Industrialists and urban dwellers forced their abolition.

questions.questionText: Rinderpest, which struck Africa in the 1890s, was:
questions.hint: It devastated the livelihoods of African herders.
questions.explanation: Rinderpest was a fast-spreading disease of cattle plague that hit Africa in the late 1880s, killing about 90 per cent of the cattle and destroying African livelihoods.

questions.questionText: Rinderpest reached Africa through:
questions.optionC: infected cattle imported from British Asia to feed Italian soldiers invading Eritrea
questions.hint: It arrived with animals brought in to feed an invading army.
questions.explanation: Rinderpest arrived in Africa in the late 1880s, carried by infected cattle imported from British Asia to feed Italian soldiers invading Eritrea in East Africa.

questions.questionText: An indentured labourer was:
questions.optionD: a bonded labourer under contract to work for an employer for a specific period to pay off his passage
questions.hint: The contract was in exchange for the cost of travel to a new country.
questions.explanation: Indentured labour is a bonded labourer under contract to work for an employer for a specific amount of time, to pay off his passage to a new country or home.

questions.questionText: Most Indian indentured workers in the nineteenth century came from:
questions.optionA: eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, central India and the dry districts of Tamil Nadu
questions.hint: The main recruiting grounds lay across the eastern and central plains and the far south.
questions.explanation: In the nineteenth century hundreds of thousands of Indian indentured workers went to work on plantations and mines. Most came from eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, central India and the dry districts of Tamil Nadu.

questions.questionText: 'Hosay' in Trinidad was:
questions.optionB: the annual Muharram procession turned into a riotous carnival
questions.hint: It shows how migrants reshaped their traditions in a new land.
questions.explanation: In Trinidad the annual Muharram procession was transformed into a riotous carnival called Hosay, in which workers of all races and religions joined.

questions.questionText: The Indian indentured labour system was abolished in:
questions.hint: It was abolished after nationalist criticism from 1900 onwards.
questions.explanation: From the 1900s India's nationalist leaders began opposing the system of indentured labour migration as abusive and cruel. It was abolished in 1921.

questions.questionText: Canal colonies in Punjab were developed mainly to:
questions.optionC: settle indentured labourers returning from abroad
questions.optionD: irrigate wasteland and grow wheat and cotton for export
questions.hint: The purpose was to turn dry land into productive export agriculture.
questions.explanation: In Punjab the British built a network of irrigation canals to transform semi-desert wastes into fertile agricultural lands that could grow wheat and cotton for export.

questions.questionText: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
questions.hint: Match each term to the region where it had its main impact.
questions.explanation: Rinderpest was the cattle plague that struck Africa in the 1890s. The Corn Laws were British, Hosay was celebrated in Trinidad, and El Dorado was a South American legend.

questions.questionText: The scrapping of the Corn Laws in Britain led to:
questions.optionB: food being imported into Britain more cheaply than it could be produced there
questions.hint: Consider what happens when cheap imports are allowed in.
questions.explanation: After the Corn Laws were scrapped, food could be imported into Britain more cheaply than it could be produced within the country. British agriculture was unable to compete and vast areas of land were left uncultivated.

tests.title: Making of a Global World – Test 4 (Beyond Board Scope – Project Work)

questions.questionText: Henry Ford adapted the assembly line for his car plant in Detroit from:
questions.hint: He borrowed the idea from an industry that dismantled rather than assembled.
questions.explanation: Henry Ford adapted the assembly line of a Chicago slaughterhouse, where animals were dressed by butchers as the carcass moved along a conveyor, to his new car plant in Detroit.

questions.questionText: The Great Depression began around:
questions.hint: It followed the boom years of the 1920s in the United States.
questions.explanation: The Great Depression began around 1929 and lasted till the mid-1930s. During this period most parts of the world experienced catastrophic declines in production, employment, incomes and trade.

questions.questionText: Which of the following was a cause of the Great Depression?
questions.optionA: Agricultural overproduction and falling prices, worsened by the withdrawal of US loans
questions.optionB: A shortage of manufactured goods worldwide
questions.optionC: The abolition of the Corn Laws
questions.optionD: A sudden rise in agricultural prices
questions.hint: Two of these worked together: too much produce and too little credit.
questions.explanation: Agricultural overproduction remained a problem, made worse by falling prices. As prices slumped and agricultural incomes declined, farmers tried to expand production, worsening the glut. The withdrawal of US loans deepened the crisis.

questions.questionText: The Bretton Woods conference of July 1944 was held at Bretton Woods in:
questions.hint: The venue was in the north-eastern United States.
questions.explanation: The Bretton Woods conference was held in July 1944 at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire, USA, to establish a framework for the post-war international economic system.

questions.questionText: The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank are together referred to as the:
questions.hint: They were founded at the same conference.
questions.explanation: The IMF and the World Bank were set up at the Bretton Woods conference and commenced financial operations in 1947. They are referred to as the Bretton Woods twins.

questions.questionText: The Bretton Woods system was based on:
questions.hint: The system tied national currencies to a fixed value.
questions.explanation: The Bretton Woods system was based on fixed exchange rates. National currencies were pegged to the dollar at a fixed exchange rate, and the dollar was anchored to gold at a fixed price.

questions.questionText: The Group of 77 (G-77) demanded:
questions.optionB: the revival of the silk routes
questions.optionC: the end of the assembly line
questions.optionD: the abolition of the Corn Laws
questions.hint: The demand concerned control over resources and fairer prices.
questions.explanation: Developing countries organised themselves as the Group of 77 to demand a new international economic order, a system that would give them real control over their natural resources, more development assistance and fairer prices for raw materials.

questions.questionText: The First World War was fought between the Allies and the Central Powers. The Central Powers included:
questions.hint: Recall which bloc Germany belonged to.
questions.explanation: The First World War was fought between the Allies — Britain, France and Russia, later joined by the US — and the Central Powers, namely Germany, Austria-Hungary and Ottoman Turkey.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): The Great Depression hit India's export trade hard.
Reason (R): Between 1928 and 1934 India's exports and imports nearly halved and agricultural prices fell sharply.
questions.optionA: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionB: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionC: A is true, but R is false.
questions.optionD: A is false, but R is true.
questions.hint: Consider what the figures for trade and prices in those years show.
questions.explanation: The Depression immediately affected Indian trade. India's exports and imports nearly halved between 1928 and 1934, and as international prices crashed, prices in India also plunged. Both statements are true and R explains A.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): In the 1920s, mass production in the United States was accompanied by a boom in the purchase of cars and household goods such as refrigerators.
Reason (R): These goods were distributed free to workers by their employers.
questions.optionA: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionB: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionC: A is true, but R is false.
questions.optionD: A is false, but R is true.
questions.hint: Check how ordinary families actually paid for these new goods.
questions.explanation: The assertion is true: there was a housing and consumer boom in 1920s America. The reason is false: a large part of these purchases was made on hire purchase, that is, on credit repaid in weekly or monthly instalments, not through free distribution.

tests.title: Age of Industrialisation – Test 1 (Periodic Assessment Only)

questions.questionText: Proto-industrialisation refers to:
questions.optionA: large-scale industrial production for an international market not based on factories
questions.optionD: the earliest use of steam power in factories
questions.hint: It describes industrial production before the factory age.
questions.explanation: Even before factories began to dot the landscape in England and Europe, there was large-scale industrial production for an international market that was not based on factories. Historians refer to this phase as proto-industrialisation.

questions.questionText: In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, merchants from European towns moved to the countryside because:
questions.optionB: urban crafts and trade guilds controlled production, competition and prices in the towns
questions.hint: Think about who controlled production inside the towns.
questions.explanation: In towns, urban crafts and trade guilds were powerful. These were associations of producers that restricted the entry of new people into the trade and controlled production, competition and prices. Merchants therefore turned to the countryside.

questions.questionText: The earliest factories in England came up by:
questions.hint: They appeared well before the nineteenth century.
questions.explanation: The earliest factories in England came up by the 1730s, though it was only in the late eighteenth century that the number of factories multiplied.

questions.questionText: Which was the first symbol of the new era of factories?
questions.hint: Its production boomed in the late eighteenth century.
questions.explanation: Cotton was the first symbol of the new era. Its production boomed in the late nineteenth century, and a series of inventions increased the efficiency of each step of the production process.

questions.questionText: Who brought the costly new machines of the textile industry together under one roof and management?
questions.hint: Bringing the machines together allowed the whole process to be supervised.
questions.explanation: Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill, bringing together the costly new machines under one roof and management so that the production process could be carefully supervised.

questions.questionText: The spinning jenny was devised in 1764 by:
questions.hint: The machine sped up the spinning process and reduced labour demand.
questions.explanation: The spinning jenny, devised by James Hargreaves in 1764, sped up the spinning process and reduced labour demand, which is why women who survived on hand spinning attacked the new machines.

questions.questionText: James Watt improved the steam engine and patented the new engine in:
questions.hint: The patent came in the early 1780s.
questions.explanation: James Watt improved the steam engine produced by Newcomen and patented the new engine in 1781.

questions.questionText: Who marketed the new steam engine produced by James Watt?
questions.hint: He was an industrialist who financed and sold the invention.
questions.explanation: The industrialist Matthew Boulton manufactured and marketed the new steam engine produced by James Watt.

questions.questionText: In Victorian Britain, many industrialists preferred hand labour over machines because:
questions.optionA: labour was abundant and wages were low
questions.optionD: hand-made goods were of poorer quality
questions.hint: Consider the supply of workers in nineteenth-century Britain.
questions.explanation: In Victorian Britain there was no shortage of human labour. Poor peasants and vagrants moved to the cities in large numbers, so wages were low and industrialists had no problem of labour shortage or high wage costs.

questions.questionText: Which of the following was NOT among the traditional industries that continued to employ large numbers in nineteenth-century Britain?
questions.hint: One of these belongs to the twentieth century.
questions.explanation: Traditional industries such as food processing, building, pottery, glass work, tanning and furniture making continued to employ large numbers. Automobile manufacture came much later.

tests.title: Age of Industrialisation – Test 2 (Periodic Assessment Only)

questions.questionText: Workers in the woollen industry attacked the Spinning Jenny mainly because:
questions.optionA: women who survived on hand spinning feared it would make them jobless
questions.optionB: it was too expensive to buy
questions.hint: Consider who lost work when the machine arrived.
questions.explanation: In the woollen industry, women who survived on hand spinning began attacking the new machines, fearing that the spinning jenny would leave them without work. The conflict over the jenny continued for a long time.

questions.questionText: Which was the main pre-colonial Indian port for trade with the Gulf and the Red Sea?
questions.hint: The port lay on the western coast of India.
questions.explanation: Surat on the Gujarat coast connected India to the Gulf and Red Sea ports, while Masulipatam on the Coromandel coast and Hooghly in Bengal had trade links with Southeast Asian ports.

questions.questionText: As European companies gained power, which ports grew at the expense of the older ones?
questions.hint: The new ports were the bases of European trading power.
questions.explanation: Trade through the old ports of Surat and Hooghly declined, while exports from Bombay and Calcutta grew, signifying the growth of colonial power.

questions.questionText: A gomastha was:
questions.optionD: a paid servant appointed by the Company to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine cloth quality
questions.hint: The Company appointed them to bypass existing traders.
questions.explanation: The Company appointed a paid servant called the gomastha to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine the quality of cloth, as part of its effort to eliminate existing traders and brokers.

questions.questionText: The Company's new system of management aimed to:
questions.optionA: eliminate the existing traders and brokers connected with the cloth trade
questions.optionD: increase the profits of Indian merchants
questions.hint: Consider who stood between the Company and the weavers.
questions.explanation: The Company established a system of management and control that would eliminate competition, control costs and ensure regular supplies. It appointed gomasthas to bypass the existing traders and brokers connected with the cloth trade.

questions.questionText: The first cotton mill in Bombay came up in:
questions.hint: It came up in the mid-1850s, just before the first jute mill in Bengal.
questions.explanation: The first cotton mill in Bombay came up in 1854 and went into production two years later.

questions.questionText: The first jute mill in Bengal was set up in:
questions.hint: It followed shortly after the first Bombay cotton mill.
questions.explanation: By 1855 the first jute mill had come up in Bengal, and another one followed seven years later in 1862.

questions.questionText: Dwarkanath Tagore made his fortune in:
questions.optionD: the China trade before turning to industry
questions.hint: His early wealth came from the eastern export trade.
questions.explanation: Dwarkanath Tagore made his fortune in the China trade before he turned to industry, setting up six joint-stock companies in the 1830s and 1840s.

questions.questionText: Who set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta in 1917?
questions.hint: He was a Marwari businessman.
questions.explanation: Seth Hukumchand, a Marwari businessman who traded with China, set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta in 1917.

questions.questionText: Which Parsi businessmen built huge industrial empires in India?
questions.hint: Both accumulated their initial wealth partly from exports to China.
questions.explanation: Parsis such as Dinshaw Petit and Jamsetjee Jeejeebhoy built huge industrial empires in India, accumulating their initial wealth partly from exports to China and partly from raw cotton shipments to England.

tests.title: Age of Industrialisation – Test 3 (Periodic Assessment Only)

questions.questionText: Which category of employee acted as a link between the industrialist and the workers?
questions.hint: He recruited workers from his own village.
questions.explanation: Industrialists usually employed a jobber to get new recruits. The jobber was an old and trusted worker who got people from his village, ensured them jobs, helped them settle in the city and provided them money in times of crisis.

questions.questionText: Most Indian industrialists in the nineteenth century accumulated their initial capital from:
questions.optionB: trade with China and other export trade
questions.hint: Their wealth came from carrying goods across the sea.
questions.explanation: Many Indian businessmen accumulated wealth from trade with China, from the export of opium and from shipments of raw cotton to England, and later invested this capital in industry.

questions.questionText: The Indian textile industry received a boost during the First World War because:
questions.optionA: new inventions were introduced in India
questions.optionC: Manchester imports into India declined and Indian mills supplied war needs
questions.hint: Consider what happened to British factories during the war.
questions.explanation: With British mills busy with war production, Manchester imports into India declined. Indian mills had a vast home market to supply and were also called upon to supply war needs. Industrial production boomed.

questions.questionText: How did the Swadeshi movement affect Indian industry?
questions.optionB: It encouraged the import of Manchester cloth
questions.optionC: It reduced the demand for Indian goods
questions.optionD: Nationalists boycotted foreign cloth, increasing the demand for Indian products
questions.hint: Recall what nationalists asked people to boycott.
questions.explanation: As the Swadeshi movement gathered momentum, nationalists mobilised people to boycott foreign cloth. Industrial groups organised themselves to protect their collective interests and pressurised the government to increase tariff protection.

questions.questionText: Manufacturers put labels and calendars with images of gods on their goods in order to:
questions.optionA: make the product appear familiar and desirable, and associate it with something divine
questions.hint: Think about how images persuade a buyer to trust a product.
questions.explanation: Images of gods and goddesses on labels and calendars were meant to make the product appear familiar and its use seem desirable, and to give divine approval to the goods being sold.

questions.questionText: Indian handloom weaving survived alongside mill production mainly because:
questions.optionA: mills were banned from making certain cloth
questions.optionB: weavers shifted to coarser and specialised weaves that mills could not easily supply
questions.optionC: handloom cloth was cheaper than mill cloth
questions.hint: Consider what kind of cloth the mills could not readily produce.
questions.explanation: Weavers survived by producing coarse cloth bought by the poor and specialised weaves such as Banarasi or Baluchari saris with borders and designs that mills could not easily imitate.

questions.questionText: Which technological change helped Indian weavers improve their productivity in the twentieth century?
questions.hint: It was a device moved by ropes and pulleys, fitted to handlooms.
questions.explanation: The fly shuttle, a mechanical device used for weaving and moved by means of ropes and pulleys, increased productivity per worker, speeded up production and reduced labour demand on Indian handlooms.

questions.questionText: European Managing Agencies that dominated Indian industry mainly:
questions.optionD: mobilised capital, set up joint-stock companies and controlled tea, coffee, mining and jute
questions.hint: They controlled the sectors where the colonial economy earned most.
questions.explanation: European Managing Agencies such as Bird Heiglers & Co., Andrew Yule and Jardine Skinner & Co. mobilised capital, set up joint-stock companies and managed them. They were mostly interested in tea and coffee plantations, and in mining, indigo and jute.

questions.questionText: Indian industrialists in the early twentieth century avoided competing with Manchester goods in the Indian market by:
questions.optionA: producing coarse cotton yarn rather than fabric, much of which was exported to China
questions.optionC: closing their mills during the war
questions.hint: Their early output went abroad rather than into cloth for India.
questions.explanation: Early cotton mills in India produced coarse cotton yarn rather than fabric. Yarn produced in Indian spinning mills was used by handloom weavers in India or exported to China, so it did not compete directly with imported cloth.

questions.questionText: By the first decade of the twentieth century, a series of changes affected the pattern of industrialisation in India. One of them was:
questions.optionA: the closure of all Indian mills
questions.optionB: the shift from yarn to cloth production as the swadeshi movement gathered momentum
questions.optionC: a ban on Indian cotton exports
questions.optionD: the end of the jute industry
questions.hint: The change followed the nationalist boycott of foreign cloth.
questions.explanation: As the swadeshi movement gathered momentum, nationalists mobilised people to boycott foreign cloth, and industrial groups pressurised the government for tariff protection. Indian mills shifted from yarn to cloth production.

tests.title: Age of Industrialisation – Test 4 (Periodic Assessment Only)

questions.questionText: The 'fly shuttle' was:
questions.optionB: a mechanical device used for weaving, moved by ropes and pulleys
questions.optionD: a printing press for cloth labels
questions.hint: It was fitted to handlooms rather than to factory machines.
questions.explanation: The fly shuttle is a mechanical device used for weaving, moved by means of ropes and pulleys. It places the horizontal threads into the vertical threads, and allows weavers to operate large looms and weave wide pieces of cloth.

questions.questionText: Which statement about industrialisation is correct?
questions.optionA: New technology was adopted immediately by all industrialists
questions.optionB: It brought rapid and dramatic technological change everywhere
questions.optionC: Hand technology and small-scale production remained important in many sectors
questions.optionD: All hand labour disappeared within a few decades
questions.hint: Consider how slowly new machines actually spread.
questions.explanation: Industrialisation did not mean a rapid or dramatic technological change everywhere. New technology spread slowly, and hand technology and small-scale production remained an important part of the industrial landscape.

questions.questionText: Manchester goods flooded the Indian market in the nineteenth century mainly because:
questions.optionA: they were machine-made and cheap, and British goods entered India duty-free while Indian goods faced tariffs in Britain
questions.optionB: Indian weavers refused to produce cloth
questions.optionD: they were hand-woven and of finer quality
questions.hint: Two advantages worked together: lower cost and favourable tariffs.
questions.explanation: Cotton weavers in India faced two problems at the same time: their export market collapsed, and the local market shrank as it was glutted with cheap machine-made Manchester imports, while British manufacturers pressurised the government to impose import duties on Indian textiles entering Britain.

questions.questionText: The First World War affected Indian industrial production by:
questions.optionB: boosting it, as mills ran multiple shifts and new factories were set up
questions.hint: Wartime demand and reduced imports worked in India's favour.
questions.explanation: Over the war years industrial production boomed. New factories were set up, old ones ran multiple shifts, and many new workers were employed as Indian mills supplied war needs and filled the gap left by declining Manchester imports.

questions.questionText: Which industries employed the largest number of workers in India by the early twentieth century?
questions.hint: One was centred in Bombay, the other in Bengal.
questions.explanation: The cotton industry, concentrated in Bombay and Ahmedabad, and the jute industry of Bengal were the two largest employers of industrial workers in India in this period.

questions.questionText: Why did small-scale industries continue to predominate in India even in the twentieth century?
questions.optionA: There was no demand for factory goods
questions.optionC: Large industries were banned by law
questions.optionD: Only a small proportion of the total industrial labour force worked in registered factories, and handicrafts production actually expanded
questions.hint: Consider what share of workers were actually in registered factories.
questions.explanation: Large industries formed only a small segment of the economy. A small proportion of the total industrial labour force worked in registered factories, while the rest worked in small workshops and household units, and handicrafts production actually expanded in the twentieth century.

questions.questionText: Which of the following best describes the position of weavers under the Company's gomastha system?
questions.optionA: Weavers lost the space to bargain, had to take loans and were paid miserably low prices
questions.optionB: Weavers were free to sell to any buyer
questions.optionC: Weavers were given land in return for cloth
questions.optionD: Weavers gained bargaining power and higher prices
questions.hint: Consider what taking an advance meant for a weaver's freedom.
questions.explanation: Once a weaver took a loan he could not sell the cloth to any other buyer and had to hand it over to the gomastha, receiving miserably low prices. In many villages this led to clashes between weavers and gomasthas.

questions.questionText: Advertisements in colonial India were important for Manchester manufacturers because:
questions.optionB: they made Manchester goods appear familiar and desirable to Indian buyers
questions.optionC: they were required by Indian law
questions.optionD: they replaced the need for shipping
questions.hint: Think about how a foreign product is made to feel local.
questions.explanation: When Manchester industrialists began selling cloth in India, they put labels on the bundles. Images of Indian gods and figures of important personages were used to make the goods seem familiar, and to give them an approved, desirable image.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): Indian handloom weavers faced a severe crisis in the nineteenth century.
Reason (R): Cheap machine-made Manchester imports flooded the Indian market while exports of Indian cotton goods declined.
questions.optionA: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionB: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionC: A is true, but R is false.
questions.optionD: A is false, but R is true.
questions.hint: Consider what happened to both the export market and the home market for Indian cloth.
questions.explanation: Weavers faced two problems at once: their export market collapsed and the local market was glutted with cheap machine-made imports. Both statements are true and R explains A.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): Industrialists in Victorian Britain quickly replaced all hand labour with machines.
Reason (R): Machines were expensive, their repair was costly and they were often not as effective as their inventors claimed.
questions.optionA: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionB: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionC: A is true, but R is false.
questions.optionD: A is false, but R is true.
questions.hint: Weigh whether the second statement supports or contradicts the first.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false. Industrialists were often reluctant to introduce machines, and hand labour remained widespread. The reason correctly states why they hesitated, so it contradicts rather than explains the assertion.

chapters.chapterName: Print Culture and the Modern World

tests.title: Print Culture and the Modern World – Test 1 (Basics)

questions.questionText: The earliest kind of print technology was developed in:
questions.hint: It began in East Asia, long before Europe.
questions.explanation: The earliest kind of print technology was developed in China, Japan and Korea. This was a system of hand printing.

questions.questionText: Hand printing in China began around AD 594, when books were printed by:
questions.optionB: rubbing paper against the inked surface of woodblocks
questions.hint: The method used carved blocks of wood.
questions.explanation: From AD 594 onwards, books in China were printed by rubbing paper against the inked surface of woodblocks. Chinese books were folded and stitched at the side in the accordion style.

questions.questionText: The oldest Japanese printed book is:
questions.hint: It is a Buddhist text from AD 868.
questions.explanation: The oldest Japanese book, printed in AD 868, is the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, containing six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations.

questions.questionText: Knowledge of woodblock printing was brought back to Italy in 1295 by:
questions.hint: He was a great explorer returning from years in China.
questions.explanation: In 1295 Marco Polo, a great explorer, returned to Italy after many years of exploration in China and brought the knowledge of woodblock printing with him.

questions.questionText: The first printing press in Europe was developed by:
questions.hint: He was the son of a merchant from Strasbourg.
questions.explanation: Johann Gutenberg developed the first known printing press in Europe in the 1430s, drawing on his knowledge of the olive and wine presses of his time.

questions.questionText: Gutenberg's printing press was modelled on the:
questions.hint: The design came from a machine used to extract oil.
questions.explanation: Gutenberg adapted existing technology to design his innovation. The olive press provided the model for the printing press, and moulds were used for casting the metal types.

questions.questionText: The first book Gutenberg printed was:
questions.hint: It was the most important religious text of the age.
questions.explanation: The first book Gutenberg printed was the Bible. About 180 copies were printed, and it took three years to produce them.

questions.questionText: Roughly how many copies of his first printed book did Gutenberg produce in three years?
questions.hint: By modern standards the number was very small.
questions.explanation: About 180 copies of the first book Gutenberg printed were produced, and it took three years to complete them, which by the standards of the time was fast production.

questions.questionText: Between 1450 and 1550, printing presses were set up in:
questions.hint: The technology spread rapidly across the continent in a century.
questions.explanation: In the hundred years between 1450 and 1550, printing presses were set up in most countries of Europe. Printers from Germany travelled to other countries, seeking work and helping to start new presses.

questions.questionText: The shift from hand printing to mechanical printing is known as:
questions.hint: The phrase describes a change in technology and its consequences.
questions.explanation: The shift from hand printing to mechanical printing led to the print revolution, which transformed the lives of people, changing their relationship to information and knowledge.

tests.title: Print Culture and the Modern World – Test 2 (Print in Europe)
