questions.questionText: In 1517, Martin Luther wrote the Ninety Five Theses criticising:
questions.optionA: the practices and rituals of the Roman Catholic Church
questions.optionB: the invention of the printing press
questions.hint: His challenge was directed at the Church of his time.
questions.explanation: In 1517 the religious reformer Martin Luther wrote Ninety Five Theses criticising many of the practices and rituals of the Roman Catholic Church, and challenged the Church to debate his ideas.

questions.questionText: Martin Luther's writings led directly to:
questions.optionA: the founding of the Deoband Seminary
questions.optionB: a division within the Church and the beginning of the Protestant Reformation
questions.optionC: the invention of the cylindrical press
questions.hint: The consequence was a permanent split in Western Christianity.
questions.explanation: Luther's translation of the New Testament and his writings spread rapidly in print. This led to a division within the Church and to the beginning of the Protestant Reformation.

questions.questionText: The Roman Church began maintaining an Index of Prohibited Books from:
questions.hint: It came several decades after Luther's Theses.
questions.explanation: Troubled by the effects of popular readings and questionings of faith, the Roman Church imposed severe controls over publishers and booksellers and began to maintain an Index of Prohibited Books from 1558.

questions.questionText: Menocchio, a miller in sixteenth-century Italy, was executed because he:
questions.optionA: refused to pay taxes to the Church
questions.optionD: reformulated the message of the Bible in a way that angered the Roman Church
questions.hint: His offence was one of interpretation, not of printing.
questions.explanation: Menocchio, a miller in Italy, reinterpreted the message of the Bible and formulated a view of God and Creation that enraged the Roman Catholic Church. He was hauled up twice and ultimately executed.

questions.questionText: In France, low-priced small books printed on poor quality paper and bound in cheap covers were called:
questions.hint: The name comes from the colour of the binding.
questions.explanation: In France were published the 'Biliotheque Bleue', which were low-priced small books printed on poor quality paper and bound in cheap blue covers.

questions.questionText: In England, penny chapbooks were carried and sold by petty pedlars known as:
questions.hint: Their name is the root of the word chapbook.
questions.explanation: In England, penny chapbooks were carried by petty pedlars known as chapmen, and sold for a penny, so that even the poor could buy them.

questions.questionText: Who wrote that 'The printing press is the most powerful engine of progress'?
questions.hint: He was an eighteenth-century French novelist.
questions.explanation: The French novelist Louise-Sébastien Mercier declared that the printing press is the most powerful engine of progress, and that public opinion would sweep despotism away.

questions.questionText: Which scholar feared that print would spread irreligious and rebellious thoughts?
questions.hint: He was a Latin scholar and a Catholic reformer who nonetheless distrusted print.
questions.explanation: Erasmus, a Latin scholar and Catholic reformer, expressed a deep anxiety about printing, arguing that while some books brought knowledge, others might be irreligious and could spread rebellious thoughts.

questions.questionText: In the mid-nineteenth century, Richard M. Hoe perfected the:
questions.optionA: power-driven cylindrical press capable of printing 8,000 sheets per hour
questions.hint: The machine was especially useful for printing newspapers.
questions.explanation: Richard M. Hoe of New York perfected the power-driven cylindrical press by the mid-nineteenth century. It was capable of printing 8,000 sheets per hour and was particularly useful for printing newspapers.

questions.questionText: The 'Shilling Series' in England brought out:
questions.optionB: cheap paperback editions of popular works
questions.hint: The name refers to the low price of each volume.
questions.explanation: In the 1920s in England, popular works were sold in cheap series called the Shilling Series. The dust cover or book jacket is also a twentieth-century innovation.

tests.title: Print Culture and the Modern World – Test 3 (Print in India)

questions.questionText: India's first printing press arrived in Goa in the mid-sixteenth century with:
questions.hint: They came to spread their faith as well as to trade.
questions.explanation: The printing press first came to Goa with Portuguese missionaries in the mid-sixteenth century. Jesuit priests learnt Konkani and printed several tracts.

questions.questionText: The first Tamil book was printed at Cochin in:
questions.hint: It came a few decades after the press reached Goa.
questions.explanation: Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book in 1579 at Cochin, and in 1713 the first Malayalam book was printed by them.

questions.questionText: India's first English newspaper, the Bengal Gazette, was brought out from 1780 by:
questions.hint: He described his paper as a commercial paper open to all but influenced by none.
questions.explanation: From 1780, James Augustus Hickey began to edit the Bengal Gazette, a weekly magazine that described itself as a commercial paper open to all, but influenced by none.

questions.questionText: The newspaper Sambad Kaumudi was published from 1821 by:
questions.hint: He was a social reformer who campaigned against sati.
questions.explanation: Rammohun Roy published the Sambad Kaumudi from 1821. From 1822, two Persian newspapers were published, Jam-i-Jahan Nama and Shamsul Akhbar.

questions.questionText: Which newspaper did orthodox Hindus bring out to oppose reformist opinions on widow immolation?
questions.hint: It was published specifically as a counter to reformist views.
questions.explanation: Orthodox Hindus brought out the Samachar Chandrika to oppose reformist opinions, including those on the immolation of widows.

questions.questionText: The Deoband Seminary, founded in 1867, published:
questions.optionB: thousands of fatwas telling Muslim readers how to conduct themselves in everyday life
questions.hint: The publications concerned everyday conduct and the meaning of doctrine.
questions.explanation: The Deoband Seminary, founded in 1867, published thousands upon thousands of fatwas telling Muslim readers how to conduct themselves in their everyday lives, and explaining the meanings of Islamic doctrines.

questions.questionText: The Vernacular Press Act was passed in:
questions.hint: It followed the growing assertiveness of the Indian-language press.
questions.explanation: In 1878 the Vernacular Press Act was passed, modelled on the Irish Press Laws. It provided the government with extensive rights to censor reports and editorials in the vernacular press.

questions.questionText: The Vernacular Press Act was modelled on the press laws of which other part of the British Empire?
questions.hint: The model came from an island close to Britain itself.
questions.explanation: The Vernacular Press Act was modelled on the Irish Press Laws. It gave the government extensive rights to censor reports and editorials in the vernacular press.

questions.questionText: Who published the newspaper Kesari and was imprisoned in 1908?
questions.hint: His imprisonment provoked widespread protests across India.
questions.explanation: When Bal Gangadhar Tilak wrote with sympathy about the Punjab revolutionaries in Kesari, he was imprisoned in 1908, provoking in turn widespread protests all over India.

questions.questionText: The first printed edition of Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas came out from Calcutta in:
questions.hint: It appeared in the early nineteenth century.
questions.explanation: The first printed edition of Tulsidas's sixteenth-century text Ramcharitmanas came out from Calcutta in 1810. By the mid-nineteenth century, cheap lithographic editions flooded north Indian markets.

tests.title: Print Culture and the Modern World – Test 4 (Mixed & Application)

questions.questionText: Rashsundari Debi's 'Amar Jiban' (1876) is important because it was:
questions.optionC: the first full-length autobiography published in the Bengali language
questions.hint: She was a housewife who taught herself to read in secret.
questions.explanation: Rashsundari Debi, a young married girl in a very orthodox household, learnt to read in the secrecy of her kitchen and later wrote her autobiography Amar Jiban, published in 1876. It was the first full-length autobiography published in the Bengali language.

questions.questionText: 'Stripurushtulna', criticising the social differences between men and women, was written by:
questions.hint: The author was a woman writing from Maharashtra.
questions.explanation: Tarabai Shinde, educated at home in Poona, published Stripurushtulna, a book in which she criticised the social differences between men and women.

questions.questionText: Jyotiba Phule's 'Gulamgiri' (1871) wrote about:
questions.optionA: the injustices of the caste system
questions.hint: The title itself means slavery.
questions.explanation: Jyotiba Phule, the Maratha pioneer of low-caste protest movements, wrote about the injustices of the caste system in his Gulamgiri, published in 1871.

questions.questionText: Cheap books printed in the Battala area of north Calcutta were:
questions.optionB: sold in local markets and by hawkers, and were popular among women readers
questions.hint: They circulated among ordinary households rather than official circles.
questions.explanation: By the late nineteenth century a lot of cheap books were being printed in the Battala area of north Calcutta and sold in local markets, hawked by pedlars. Many of them were bought by women who read them in their leisure time.

questions.questionText: Which press in Lucknow published a large number of religious texts in vernacular languages?
questions.hint: It was based in Lucknow, not Bombay.
questions.explanation: The Naval Kishore Press at Lucknow and the Shri Venkateshwar Press in Bombay published numerous religious texts in vernaculars, often in the everyday language of ordinary people.

questions.questionText: What did Mahatma Gandhi say in 1922 about the liberty of the press?
questions.optionA: That newspapers should be banned during a movement
questions.optionB: That only English newspapers should be allowed
questions.optionC: That it was of no importance to the national movement
questions.optionD: That the liberty of speech, of the press and of association were among the most powerful vehicles of expressing and cultivating public opinion
questions.hint: He named three liberties together and called them powerful vehicles.
questions.explanation: In 1922 Gandhi said that liberty of speech, liberty of the press and freedom of association were the three most powerful vehicles of expressing and cultivating public opinion, and that fighting for swaraj meant fighting for these liberties above all.

questions.questionText: Which of the following best describes how print helped nationalist ideas in India?
questions.optionA: It allowed news of colonial misrule to circulate widely and encouraged nationalist debate across regions
questions.optionB: It was used only for religious books
questions.optionC: It reached only the English-educated elite
questions.optionD: It was controlled entirely by the government and could not spread new ideas
questions.hint: Consider what happened when reports from one region reached another.
questions.explanation: From the 1820s the vernacular press reported on colonial misrule and encouraged nationalist activities. Papers in one region reported the news of other regions, creating a sense of shared struggle and provoking nationalist debate.

questions.questionText: Which of these was a nineteenth-century innovation that made books more affordable to ordinary readers?
questions.optionB: Circulating and lending libraries, and cheap serialised novels in periodicals
questions.hint: Think of ways of reading a book without buying it outright.
questions.explanation: From the early nineteenth century, lending libraries in England became instruments for educating white-collar workers, artisans and lower-middle-class people. Novels were also serialised in periodicals, which made them cheaper to read.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): Print created the possibility of a new kind of public that could debate and discuss ideas.
Reason (R): Printed books were cheaper than manuscripts and could reach a much wider readership.
questions.optionA: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionB: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionC: A is true, but R is false.
questions.optionD: A is false, but R is true.
questions.hint: Consider what changed once books could be produced in large numbers at low cost.
questions.explanation: Printing reduced the cost of books and multiplied copies, so books reached ever-wider sections of people. This created a new reading public and a new culture of debate and discussion. Both statements are true and R explains A.

questions.questionText:
Assertion (A): Handwritten manuscripts continued to be produced in India even after the introduction of print.
Reason (R): Manuscripts were expensive, fragile and had to be handled carefully.
questions.optionA: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionB: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
questions.optionC: A is true, but R is false.
questions.optionD: A is false, but R is true.
questions.hint: Both statements are correct, but check whether the second one explains the first.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true. However, the fragility and expense of manuscripts explain why they were difficult to use widely, not why their production continued after print arrived. R does not explain A.
